analysis.one_liner: Let homeowners in bankruptcy reduce mortgage balances on subprime and risky loans to save their homes.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let homeowners filing for Chapter 13 bankruptcy change the terms of subprime or nontraditional mortgages on their primary homes — including reducing the balance owed, extending payments up to 30 years, and setting a fixed interest rate — something bankruptcy courts could do for almost every other kind of debt but not home loans. It also waived the pre-bankruptcy credit counseling requirement for people facing foreclosure sale, curbed extra lender fees tacked on during bankruptcy, let older debtors protect $75,000 of home equity, and stopped lenders who broke consumer protection laws from collecting in bankruptcy court. The Senate Judiciary Committee reported it favorably and it sat on the Senate calendar, but no vote was ever scheduled.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing foreclosure whose mortgages were subprime or nontraditional (like interest-only or payment-shock adjustable loans). For them, bankruptcy court could cut the loan balance to the home's current value, stretch payments over up to 30 years at a fixed rate, and wipe out prepayment penalties — the difference between keeping and losing the home. Older debtors could shield $75,000 in home equity, and debtors facing foreclosure could skip mandatory credit counseling.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homeowners facing foreclosure on subprime loans

how_it_helps.text: Lets a Chapter 13 debtor reduce the balance on a subprime or nontraditional mortgage on their principal residence to the allowed secured claim, and repay over up to 30 years at a fixed rate based on the Federal Reserve's published conventional mortgage yield plus a risk premium.
If the loan is cut below the original principal and the home is sold during the plan, the lender shares in the sale proceeds, limiting the write-down's windfall to the debtor.
Waives the mandatory credit counseling requirement for a debtor whose home is scheduled for foreclosure sale.

Blocks lenders from adding fees, costs, or charges during the bankruptcy case unless they notify the court on time and the charges are lawful, reasonable, and in the original contract; collection of unnotified charges is treated as a violation of the discharge and automatic stay rules.

Lets debtors waive prepayment penalties, protects debtors' unscheduled legal claims from dismissal, lets consumer-debt bankruptcy courts hear core disputes instead of sending them to arbitration, gives debtors 55 and older a $75,000 homestead exemption, and bars collection of claims tainted by Truth in Lending Act or other consumer protection violations.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and investors holding subprime and nontraditional loans, who would recover less than the full contract balance when a court reduced the principal, receive a fixed government-benchmark interest rate instead of the contract rate, and lose fee and prepayment-penalty income. The shared-appreciation provision returns part of the loss if the home sells during the plan.

drawbacks.text: Creditors' core objection: if bankruptcy courts can cut mortgage balances and rates, lenders face larger losses on risky loans, which they said would raise interest rates and reduce credit availability for future homebuyers, including borrowers with good credit.

The committee-passed version narrowed eligibility to subprime and nontraditional mortgages, so distressed borrowers with ordinary prime loans still could not modify their home loan in bankruptcy — leaving most of the foreclosure crisis unaddressed by the main provision.
Losses on written-down loans shift to the holder's unsecured claim, meaning other creditors in the bankruptcy, and in securitized pools other investors, absorb part of the cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the families it covered, the benefit was direct and large: keeping a home instead of losing it to foreclosure. The real cost falls on loan holders, and whether that spreads into higher mortgage rates for future buyers is the strongest honest objection — though the same asymmetry (courts could rewrite every other kind of secured debt but not home mortgages) was the rule the bill aimed to fix, and lenders knowingly made the risky loans it targeted. The committee rewrite narrowing the bill to subprime and nontraditional loans reduced both its cost to lenders and its reach to homeowners.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it and put it on the Senate's calendar of bills awaiting floor action, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on October 3, 2007, with thirteen other Democratic senators joining as original sponsors, and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The committee held hearings in December 2007, ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on April 3, 2008, and held further hearings in November 2008.
On July 29, 2008, the committee reported the bill with a substitute amendment that narrowed the core provision to subprime and nontraditional mortgages, rather than all primary-residence loans.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 911), and a written report with minority views was filed on September 26, 2008.
The bill remained on the calendar without a floor vote when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and investors holding subprime and nontraditional home loans came out ahead: they avoided court-ordered principal reductions, rate caps, and fee limits, and foreclosures proceeded under the existing rules.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and led it through introduction and committee consideration.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, brought the bill to a favorable committee vote, and reported it to the Senate with an amendment and a written report.

for.name: 14 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Sponsored or cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Schumer, Dodd, Obama, Biden, Clinton, and Kerry.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Opposed letting judges reduce mortgage balances in bankruptcy and were positioned to block the bill from reaching the floor; the committee report carried minority views.

against.name: Mortgage and banking industry
against.role: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Ran a major lobbying campaign against allowing bankruptcy judges to modify home loans, arguing it would raise the cost of mortgage credit.

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote while it sat on the legislative calendar.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Senate Democrat (14 of 49), the committee report carried minority views filed by Republicans, and no floor vote ever happened; the fight lined up as Democrats for the bill, Republicans opposed, though Democratic leadership also never brought it to a vote.

industries.note: Courts could cut the principal owed on subprime and nontraditional loans, cap the interest rate at a Federal Reserve benchmark, and strip unnotified fees and prepayment penalties during bankruptcy. Servicers also lose their usual ability to tack fees onto a homeowner's balance while the case is pending.

Holders of pooled subprime and nontraditional loans would recover less when courts reduced balances, absorbing part of the loss through their unsecured claims. The bill's shared-appreciation provision returns some of that if the home sells during the bankruptcy plan.
The 2005 bankruptcy law routes every filer through paid credit counseling; this bill exempted debtors whose homes were scheduled for foreclosure sale, removing those customers from a mandated market.
Bankruptcy courts could hear core consumer-debt disputes themselves instead of referring them to arbitration under pre-dispute agreements, keeping those disputes in public court.
